title: Excess deaths in your neighbourhood during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic
meta_description: Our interactive chart lets you view data on deaths in your neighbourhood compared with the average for 2015 to 2019.

breadcrumb.text: Excess deaths in your neighbourhood during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic

lede: Some neighbourhoods saw more than twice as many residents die than would have been expected for the time of year during the spring and summer of 2020, while excess deaths were spread out over a longer period in the following autumn and winter. Our interactive chart and map let you see what happened where you live.

body.text: 3 August 2021

So far in England and Wales, there have been two periods during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic when weekly and monthly registrations of deaths from all causes were consistently higher than the five-year average – also known as “excess deaths”.

Using weekly data, the first period was from the week ending 20 March to the week ending 12 June 2020 and the second was from the week ending 11 September 2020 to the week ending 5 March 2021. Using monthly data, the periods above average were from March to July 2020 and then from September 2020 to March 2021.

Excess deaths are the clearest way to compare the likely impact of the pandemic over time, because a substantial number of non-COVID-19 excess deaths were recorded early in the pandemic, in March and April 2020. One reason for excess deaths [could be that COVID-19 was undiagnosed](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/birthsdeathsandmarriages/deaths/articles/analysisofdeathregistrationsnotinvolvingcoronaviruscovid19englandandwales28december2019to1may2020/28december2019to10july2020).

body.h2: How excess deaths have changed each month where you live
body.h4: Use your postcode to see the number of excess deaths each month where you live
body.text: Overall, the North West, London and North East [had the highest COVID-19 mortality rates in 2020](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/birthsdeathsandmarriages/deaths/articles/deathsregisteredduetocovid19/2020).

body.h2: How excess deaths have changed each month where you live
body.h4: Use your postcode to see the number of excess deaths each month where you live
body.text: At an individual neighbourhood level between March and July 2020, some of the hardest hit places for overall excess deaths were spread across the north of England, Midlands and south of England.

body.h2: How excess deaths have changed each month where you live
body.h4: Use your postcode to see the number of excess deaths each month where you live
body.text: There were around 200 neighbourhoods where the number of deaths was at least double what would normally have been expected during those five months.

body.h2: How excess deaths have changed each month where you live
body.h4: Use your postcode to see the number of excess deaths each month where you live
body.text: These included Crabtree and Fir Vale in Sheffield, which had the largest excess, with 123 deaths between March and July 2020, 77 more than the average of 46, an excess of 167%.

body.h2: How excess deaths have changed each month where you live
body.h4: Use your postcode to see the number of excess deaths each month where you live
body.text: When infections and deaths due to COVID-19 increased again in the autumn of 2020, total deaths registered in England and Wales remained above average for seven months.

body.h2: How excess deaths have changed each month where you live
body.h4: Use your postcode to see the number of excess deaths each month where you live
body.text: Between September 2020 and March 2021, the West St Leonards area of Hastings recorded 184 deaths, which was 65 (55%) more than average. Of these, 45 were registered in January 2021. This was the highest monthly excess of any neighbourhood at this time.

body.h2: Some neighbourhoods registered no coronavirus deaths
body.text: Some neighbourhoods registered no coronavirus deaths

body.h2: Some neighbourhoods registered no coronavirus deaths
body.text: Out of 7,201 neighbourhoods, there are just 13 in England and one in Wales that recorded no deaths due to COVID-19 – where coronavirus was the main cause of death - up to April 2021. Most of these were in the South West of England, including parts of Cornwall and Devon. Some are also in built-up areas and include Bristol City Centre and Leeds City Centre. One area of Manchester, Castlegate and Deansfield, also recorded no deaths due to COVID-19.

body.h2: Some neighbourhoods registered no coronavirus deaths
body.text: The only MSOA in Wales to have recorded no deaths due to COVID-19 by April 2021 was LLandudno Junction South and Llansanffraid Glan, Conwy.

body.h2: Urban areas suffered the most during the spring of 2020, but mortality rates stayed high for longer later in the pandemic
body.h4: Select your local area and see how mortality rates changed month by month
body.text: The first peak in coronavirus deaths was in April 2020, while the country was in the middle of the first national lockdown. At this time, urban centres in London, Birmingham, the north of England and South Wales had the highest rates of deaths due to any cause.

body.h2: Urban areas suffered the most during the spring of 2020, but mortality rates stayed high for longer later in the pandemic
body.h4: Select your local area and see how mortality rates changed month by month
body.text: There were many reasons why certain communities experienced high death rates, with more deaths due to COVID-19 in the [most deprived areas of England and Wales than in the least deprived areas](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/birthsdeathsandmarriages/deaths/datasets/deathsduetocovid19bylocalareaanddeprivation).

body.h2: Urban areas suffered the most during the spring of 2020, but mortality rates stayed high for longer later in the pandemic
body.h4: Select your local area and see how mortality rates changed month by month
body.text: There were also higher death rates [among some ethnic minority groups](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/birthsdeathsandmarriages/deaths/articles/updatingethniccontrastsindeathsinvolvingthecoronaviruscovid19englandandwales/24january2020to31march2021) as well as in [males](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/conditionsanddiseases/articles/coronaviruscovid19andthedifferenteffectsonmenandwomenintheukmarch2020tofebruary2021/2021-03-10) and [those with pre-existing conditions](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/birthsdeathsandmarriages/deaths/bulletins/monthlymortalityanalysisenglandandwales/april2021#pre-existing-conditions-of-people-whose-death-was-due-to-covid-19-deaths-registered-in-january-to-march-quarter-1-2021). There have also been higher death rates among people with [jobs with regular exposure to COVID-19](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/causesofdeath/bulletins/coronaviruscovid19relateddeathsbyoccupationenglandandwales/deathsregisteredbetween9marchand28december2020).

body.h2: Urban areas suffered the most during the spring of 2020, but mortality rates stayed high for longer later in the pandemic
body.h4: Select your local area and see how mortality rates changed month by month
body.text: Although overall deaths in England and Wales reduced during the summer of 2020, in some areas of northern England, such as Tameside and Blackburn with Darwen, mortality rates were higher than normal.

body.h2: Urban areas suffered the most during the spring of 2020, but mortality rates stayed high for longer later in the pandemic
body.h4: Select your local area and see how mortality rates changed month by month
body.text: The autumn and winter of 2020 saw mortality rates peak in different local areas in different months. In November 2020, mortality rates were highest in Rochdale and Blaenau Gwent and in December 2020 parts of Lincolnshire such as Lincoln and Boston recorded their highest mortality rates of the pandemic.

body.h2: Urban areas suffered the most during the spring of 2020, but mortality rates stayed high for longer later in the pandemic
body.h4: Select your local area and see how mortality rates changed month by month
body.text: As 2021 began with a third national lockdown, there were many areas in both England and Wales with high mortality rates; with the area from Essex to East London to East Sussex suffering due to the spread of the Alpha COVID-19 variant, first identified in Kent.

body.h2: Urban areas suffered the most during the spring of 2020, but mortality rates stayed high for longer later in the pandemic
body.h4: Select your local area and see how mortality rates changed month by month
body.text: In January 2021, the mortality rate in England was highest in Barking and Dagenham. In Wales, the highest was in Bridgend.

body.h2: Urban areas suffered the most during the spring of 2020, but mortality rates stayed high for longer later in the pandemic
body.h4: Select your local area and see how mortality rates changed month by month
body.text: On average, overall mortality rates in England and Wales declined in February 2021, although in some areas they were only reaching their peak. These areas included Copeland, Great Yarmouth, Bolsover and Norwich. In March 2021, Blackpool had the highest ASMR in England and Wales, but this was below its April 2020 peak.

body.h2: Urban areas suffered the most during the spring of 2020, but mortality rates stayed high for longer later in the pandemic
body.h4: Select your local area and see how mortality rates changed month by month
body.text: Since March 2021, deaths in England and Wales returned to average or near to average for the time of year, although deaths due to COVID-19 increased again in July.

body.h2: Glossary
body.h4: Age-standardised mortality rates (ASMRs)
body.text: These are used for comparisons over time and between areas rather than numbers of deaths, as ASMRs account for differences in the population size and age structure.

body.h2: Glossary
body.h4: Excess deaths
body.text: Excess deaths

body.h2: Glossary
body.h4: Excess deaths
body.text: Excess deaths in this analysis are the difference between the number of deaths registered in each period (week or month) and the same period in the five-year average (2015 to 2019). Using the average gives us a comparison of how many deaths we would expect in a "normal" year, before the COVID-19 pandemic.
